generator_view.scenario: A buyer has about forty dollars for a sister whose usual chocolate is an 85-percent dark bar. The buyer is deciding between a small set of three origin- or percentage-labeled bars and a larger assorted truffle gift box. The bar candidates include a Madagascar Manjari listing with conflicting 64- and 65-percent labels, a Peru 70-percent dark bar with puffed quinoa and Criollo language, and an Ecuador 60-percent dark-milk bar. The box candidates are one roughly 36-piece assortment of milk, dark, white, 60-percent extra-dark, fudge-swirl and sea-salt truffles and one 16-piece assortment of milk, dark and white shells with several flavored fillings. The available background says cacao percentage, origin, genetics, fermentation, drying, recipe and processing may relate to flavor but do not collapse into a single quality rank. Community discussions mention shipped birthday gifts, flavor variety, price per ounce and individual sweetness preferences, but do not test these exact gifts for this recipient. Current delivered totals, availability and arrival, complete product-by-product ingredients and allergens, dark-piece allocations and a matched recipient tasting are unresolved.
generator_view.target: Decide whether the origin and cacao-percentage labels imply real flavor differences without treating either label as a complete quality rank, then choose an evidence-bounded birthday gift within about forty dollars for a recipient who normally prefers 85-percent dark bars. Compare the exact bars and assorted truffle boxes on product form, useful dark quantity, recipe, ingredients, allergens, fillings, possible alcohol, current delivered cost and arrival protection; retain seller inconsistencies and the limited scope of ratings and community comments; explain the role and limits of origin, percentage, variety and processing evidence; and end with a small reversible recipient-tasting rule that selects only the cheapest exact path passing every gate, uses a known 85-percent reference, or defers.
